text: The effect of dimethylglyoxime on Co electrodeposition was investigated with cyclic voltammetry, chronopotentiometry, quartz microbalance as well as electrochemical impedance. A potential dependent suppression effect was observed at low potential with a breakdown of the suppression at high potential, resulting in a hysteresis in CV. The addition of dimethylglyoxime not only causes a fast and strong suppression in potential transients but also modifies the impedance spectra. Additional capacitive loops and inductance loops emerged depending on the applied potential, suggesting a competitive adsorption between different surface adsorbed intermediates. A relaxation of suppression effect was observed in absence of agitation and a strong suppression was re-established upon agitation. A reverse relation between Co deposition rate and rotation rate was observed when the rotation rate is below a critical value, providing a path to enable the preferential deposition at the bottom of a small damascene feature. © The Author(s) 2016. text: The state-of-the-art back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects are fabricated with copper, which replaced Aluminum in late 1990’s due to its lower resistivity and superior reliability. 1,2 As the interconnect continues to scale, the critical dimension of the BEOL structures has approached the electron mean free path of copper. The copper resistivity in such nanostructures increases exponentially as the dimension further shrinks, 3,4 posing tremendous challenges to the continuous scaling of copper interconnect for 7 nm technology and beyond. While the bulk resistivity of a metal is an intrinsic property of the material its resistivity in these small structures is largely determined by what happens to the electrons when they come across an interface, i.e., the surface of the metal structure in contact with the matrix materials, the boundaries between grains in the metal structure and the internal interface between metal and the embedded impurity species. 5 Metals with shorter electron mean free path are less susceptible to the effect of scaling and may appear advantageous for the interconnect application. For example, transition metals including Ni, Co, Mo and Ru were predicted to be potential candidates to replace Cu. 6

text: In addition to the advantage of a shorter mean free path, some of the candidate metals can potentially provide performance gain through innovative integration schemes. The overall resistance of an interconnect structure is a result of not only the copper but also other materials used in the interconnect structure for a variety of purposes. Such materials include diffusion barrier, adhesion layer, capping layer and sometimes additional elements as the seed layer for copper plating. Therefore, using metals that can serve dual or multiple purposes may allow more volume for the conducting metal and thus a lower overall resistance and an improved RC delay. Furthermore, new materials that enable better integration and lower defectivities can improve the overall performance as well. For example, chemical vapor deposited (CVD) and atomic layer deposited (ALD) Ru was previously studied to replace the Ta diffusion barrier – Cu seed stack. 7–9

text: Co has recently gained more and more attention as a material to replace the traditional Ta liner. 10,11 Compared with Ta, Co provides a better wettability of PVD Cu seed, enables a more conformal Cu seed coverage and therefore improves the extendibility of Cu electroplating in smaller dimensions. 12 In addition, the enhanced grain growth of Cu electroplated on Co seed 13 and the self-formation of a barrier layer enabled by the Mn diffusion through Co layer 14 potentially provide additional performance gain on the reliability of the interconnect structures.

text: Recently, selectively electroless deposited Co has been demonstrated to partially or completely replace the Cu in the small vias to improve the via resistance. 15 The bottom up fill of the via structures relied on the selectivity between the exposed underneath metal layer and the dielectrics for electroless deposition process. Electrolytic super conformal deposition of Co and Ni was reported using 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonic acid (MBIS). 16–19 A potential dependent adsorption, passivation and desorption of the additive was found to result in a negative differential resistance in cyclic voltammetry and therefore multiple steady states at certain potentials. Super conformal deposition of through silicon vias (TSV) was enabled by controlling the deposition at such potentials, where the bottom and top of a TSV are plated at two different states. Super conformal NiFe filling into sub-50 nm interconnect trenches was demonstrated with a two component additive system using a polymer suppressor and a monomer accelerator. 20 More recently, three component commercial additive has been reported for the bottom up filling of Co for interconnect. 21

text: Electrodeposition of cobalt and its alloys has been studied extensively in the past for their magnetic properties. Among them, CoNiFe 22–25 and CoFe 26–28 alloys were used in commercial hard disk drive writing heads for their low coercivities and high moments. The two additives commonly used in magnetic thin film plating, saccharin and thiourea, were studied with scanning tunneling microscope and were found to adsorb on Au(111) surface through physisorption and chemisorption respectively. 29 The different sulfur incorporation behaviors resulted in different coercivities of the deposited films.

text: A group of additives including saccharin and thiourea were previously studied for their impacts on the NiFe alloy deposition toward superconformal filling. 20 While polyethyleneimine (PEI) was found to show suppression effect, thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid showed only acceleration effect. In addition, mercapto-benezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative showed suppression followed by acceleration effect. Comparing the molecular structures of these additives in Figure 1, it is clear that PEI only has paired amine groups, which are two CH groups apart. Thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid both have mercapto groups vie an isomerization and a disproportionation reaction, 30 respectively. When both mercapto group and paired amine (or imine) groups are present in the molecules, such as mercaptobenezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative, both suppression and acceleration effects were observed. In addition, when one of the paired amine nitrogen is replaced by oxygen in mercapto-benzoxazole, the suppression effect was significantly weakened and only acceleration effect was observed. Finally, when the mercapto group was removed and only a sulfonic group is present in saccharin, neither suppression nor acceleration was observed. Based on this previous work, it can be speculated that a pair of amine (imine) group is responsible for a suppression effect and a mercapto group for acceleration.

text: In an effort to search for a suppressing additive for a onecomponent Co deposition chemistry, this paper presents a study of the effect of dimethylglyoxime (DMG) on the electrodeposition of cobalt. DMG and other dioxime have been previously used as an additive in Co electroless deposition, 31 mainly as a stabilizer due to its strong complexing with Co ^ 2 +. The structure of DMG, particularly in its complexed form with Co ^ 2 +, remotely mimics many of the molecules in Figure 1. However, DMG has only a pair of conjugated imine groups without any sulfur containing groups. The study of Co electrodeposition in presence of DMG is expected to shed light on the interactions between the conjugated pair of imine groups and the metal ions during the electrochemical reaction.

text: The effect of DMG on Co deposition was first examined with cyclic voltammetry (CV). A 100 nm layer of cobalt was deposited on Pt disc electrode in the additive free solution before each CV. A change of open circuit potential (OCP) from about 0.3 V to 0.48 V (both vs. SCE) was observed before and after this pre-plating. Potential was then swept from 0.48 V to 1.5 V with a sweep rate of 5 mV/sec. Figure 2 shows the CV curves with different amounts of DMG without and with ohmic drop correction. When no DMG was present in the solution, the cathodic deposition current started at 0.7 V and reached a current density of 2 mA/cm2 at 0.8 V and 4 mA/cm2 at 0.85 V. The forward and backward scans coincided with each other. The addition of 10 ppm DMG did not change the CV behavior. However, when 100 ppm DMG was added into the solution, the deposition was significantly polarized at low current range. The onset of the cathodic reaction did not occur until 0.9 V, after which a sudden jump of the cathodic reaction rate was observed. Furthermore, the suppressed cathodic current at low potential was not observed in the backward scan, resulting in a hysteresis in CV. Further increase of DMG concentration to 300 ppm resulted in stronger suppression of the cathodic current. This suppression was present regardless of the potential, causing a much diminished hysteresis. Figure 2b presents the same CV curves with the ohmic resistance of solution accounted for using impedance measurement. The sudden current increase in the case of 100 ppm DMG was so significant that the CV showed a S-shaped negative differential resistance after the ohmic correction.

text: In addition to CVs, potential transients during galvanostatic deposition was studied with injection of different amount of DMG at 100 rpm rotation and two current densities, 3 and 10 mA/cm2. It is evident from Figure 3 that the addition of DMG resulted in a fast and strong suppression effect. For example, the deposition potential at - 3 mA/cm2 increased by 40 mV and 100 mV within 5 seconds after the injection of 10 ppm and 90 ppm DMG into the electrolyte, respectively. Although this potential rise was an overshoot due to the stagnant flow and the potential fell back upon further homogenization, the response time was in the same order of a typical suppressor in copper damascene chemistry, 32 suggesting a fast action of DMG on Co deposition. While the additional injection of 200 ppm DMG (300 ppm in total) resulted in further suppression, experiments with DMG beyond 300 ppm showed that the suppression effect was saturated at 300 ppm. The transient at 10 mA/cm2 followed the same trend.

text: As shown in Figure 4a, Co deposition was suppressed in the presence of 100 ppm DMG. The suppression was more pronounced as the DMG concentration increased from 100 to 300 ppm. Furthermore, the sudden current increase as well as the s-shaped negative differential resistance in CVs were proved to result from Co deposition. Side reaction current densities were presented in Figure 4b. The CVs in Co-free solutions with and without DMG were included for comparison. The side reaction current density in a DMG free electrolyte coincided with the total current density of Co-free solution. However, the side reaction rates at potentials more negative than 0.9 V significantly increased when DMG was added. On the other hand, the addition of DMG didn’t change the total current density of a metal free electrolyte. Because the Pt electrode was pre-coated with a layer of Co before all experiments, the increased side reaction is believed to be a result of additional side reaction mechanism that involves not only DMG but also Co(II). For example, a catalytic effect of Co (and Ni) was reported for the reduction of DMG. 37 While the reduction of DMG into hydroxylamino-butane occurs at much higher cathodic potentials, the reduction of hydrogen in DMG molecule was found to be catalysed by the reduction of Co(II).

When less amount of DMG is used, the percentage of Co(II) in the non-complexed form is expected to be higher. In addition, even if Co(II) were complexed in the solution, this homogeneous complexation in the solution would not explain the potential dependent suppression effect in Co deposition.

text: An electrochemical quartz microbalance was used to study the electrodeposition as well as adsorption in absence of agitation. Figure 7a shows the current density and the QCM frequency at a constant voltage of 0.84 V. Upon the injection of 100 ppm DMG, the cathodic current dropped significantly from 2.3 to 1 mA/cm2. At the same time, the slope of the QCM frequency curve decreased significantly, indicating a slower metal deposition rate. A close look at the QCM frequency showed no sudden jump of the mass, which was observed upon injection of polyethylene glycol (PEG) during copper electrodeposition 45 due to the strong fast adsorption of PEG onto Cu surface. This difference suggests that the suppressing intermediate is either more light-weighted or adsorbs more slowly than PEG in the copper case. Furthermore, the current density as well as the frequency slope kept increasing again after a maximum suppression effect. This relaxation of the suppression effect was interrupted by the replenishment of solution at electrode surface using a pipette, where a strong suppression effect was re-established suggesting a depletion and replenishment of a suppressing species at the surface.

text: For a 700 sec long experiment in a solution with 0.3 ~M~CoSO_4 the maximum decay of a mass transport controlled Co deposition rate would result in a current down to 4 mA/cm2 based on the Cottrell’s equation 46 with a typical diffusion coefficient of 1 0 ^ - 5 ~cm ^ 2 / sec. The current densities observed in this experiment is far below this value and therefore the depletion of Co is not believed to occur. This is also consistent with the constant Co deposition rate observed in additive free solution. When DMG was added into the electrolyte, the formation of a surface adsorbed species, for example [Co(DMG) ], suppressed the Co deposition. However, the coverage of this adsorbed species appeared to decrease after reaching a maximum suppression effect. Therefore, this adsorbed species is believed to be broken down or be incorporated into the Co deposit. At a DMG concentration of 100 ppm the concentration of Co ( DMG) _ 2 in electrolyte was 0.4 mM with all DMG being complexed. As the surface concentration of Co(DMG) 2 in electrolyte is depleted, the equilibrium between the adsorption and consumption of [ Co ( DMG) _ 2 ] _ ads was broken and its surface coverage decreases. However, a replenishment of Co(DMG) _ 2 in electrolyte at the electrode surface increased the surface coverage of [ Co ( DMG) _ 2 ] _ ads and reestablished the strong suppression effect. Considering the application of Co deposition in small high aspect ratio structures, this agitation dependent suppressing effect can be very useful to enable a preferential deposition at the bottom of a narrow feature, where the agitation is hard to reach.

text: When a rotation rate of 400, 900, 100, and 50 rpm was applied, the current density dropped to about 0.5 mA/cm2. The higher the rotation rate, the faster the current drop. This observation was also consistent with the replenishment experiments in QCM study. A faster rotation rate results in a thinner diffusion boundary layer and a higher supply rate of Co(DMG) _ 2 to the electrode surface. The concentration of Co(DMG) 2 at the vicinity of electrode starts to restore when excessive Co(DMG) was supplied to the electrode surface. Switching off these high rotation rates caused an immediate drop in current density followed by the gradual current increase as discussed above. The immediate current drop was probably due to the decrease of side reactions, which is under mass transport control or mixed control. A higher rotation rate before the switching caused a longer delay before the current increase. This trend can also be well explained by a higher surface concentration of Co(DMG) _ 2 in the electrolyte when a higher rotation rate was used. A longer time would be needed to deplete the excessive Co(DMG) _ 2 in the electrolyte resulted from the higher rotation rate.

Three rotation rates, 25, 12 and 6 rpm, were used and the observations confirmed the expectation. Among them, the highest rotation rate of 25 rpm resulted in the most replenishment and therefore the strongest suppression. In addition, the steady state current at these low rotation rates showed more noise than higher rotation rates because of the intrinsic small fluctuation in rotation control. As discussed above, the partial replenishment and [ Co ( DMG) _ 2 ] _ ads surface coverage are expected to be highly sensitive to the rotation rates.

text: For the application of Co deposition into deep and narrow damascene trenches (or vias), agitation at the top of trench is expected to be greater than at the bottom of trench. Super conformal deposition would be expected if the agitation at these two locations were controlled at above and below the critical rotation rate, 50 rpm in this case, respectively. Because the trench depth changes as the filling continues, the rotation rate may be engineered to enable the continuous deposition at the bottom while maintaining strong suppression at the top.

text: Addition of dimethylglyoxime in a mild acid Co electrodeposition electrolyte suppressed the Co deposition rate and enhanced the side reaction. The potential dependent suppression effect resulted in an S-shape negative differential resistance in CV. A surface adsorbed species, for example [ Co ( DMG) _ 2 ] _ ads, was proposed to be responsible for the suppression. Additional capacitance and inductance loops were observed in impedance spectra upon the addition of DMG, which was consistent with the competitive adsorption between intermediate species, such as C o ( I) _ ads and [ Co(DMG) _ 2 ] _ ads ^ - A strong rapid suppression upon injection of DMG was observed in potential transients on a rotating disk electrode. However, this suppression effect was relaxed in absence of agitation. As the surface adsorbed species are consumed or decomposed along with deposition, the depletion of Co(DMG) in electrolyte at the electrode surface resulted in a decrease of [ Co ( DMG) _ 2 ] _ ads surface coverage. Replenishment of surface electrolyte re-establish the strong suppression, potentially enabling a preferential deposition at the bottom of narrow features in damascene electroplating.

The potential dependent suppression effect resulted in an S-shape negative differential resistance in CV. A surface adsorbed species, for example $[ \mathrm { C o } ( \mathrm { D M G } ) _ { 2 } ] _ { \mathrm { a d s } }$ , was proposed to be responsible for the suppression. Replenishment of surface electrolyte re-establish the strong suppression, potentially enabling a preferential deposition at the bottom of narrow features in damascene electroplating.
